lesson.title: Runs on the Bank: How Panic Emptied America's Vaults
lesson.summary: Without deposit insurance to reassure the public, waves of bank runs during the early 1930s wiped out the savings of millions of Americans and choked off the credit the economy desperately needed.
lesson.body:
Banks in this era operated on what is called fractional reserve banking: they kept only a portion of their depositors' money on hand at any given time and lent out the rest to earn interest. This system works fine as long as depositors trust that their money is safe and only a small number withdraw funds on any given day. But if depositors began to fear that a bank was in trouble, they would rush to withdraw their savings all at once, a bank run, and even a fundamentally healthy bank could not pay out every depositor simultaneously. Panic itself, in other words, could destroy a solvent institution.

No federal deposit insurance existed at the time to reassure the public, unlike the FDIC protection depositors rely on today. A rumor, a nearby bank's collapse, or simple contagious fear was often enough to start a run. Between 1930 and 1933, thousands of banks failed across the country, roughly nine thousand by commonly cited estimates, though exact counts vary somewhat depending on the source and how failures are defined. Small rural banks without diversified capital were especially vulnerable, but larger urban banks failed as well.

The consequences went far beyond the individual families who lost their life savings. As banks failed or grew fearful of failing, the ones that survived pulled back sharply on lending, a credit contraction that starved businesses and farmers of the capital they needed to operate. The nation's overall money supply shrank as a result, contributing to deflation, a general fall in prices that made existing debts effectively harder to repay in real terms. That, in turn, pushed more borrowers and more banks toward failure, a vicious spiral that deepened the Depression well beyond what the stock market crash alone had caused.

This banking crisis connects directly to the broader set of causes discussed in the previous chapter: it was not caused by the 1929 crash in any simple, direct way, but the economic contraction, falling asset prices, and eroding confidence that followed the crash created the conditions for a full-blown banking panic. Fixing this broken banking system would become one of the first and most urgent priorities of the federal government, first under Herbert Hoover and then, more decisively, under Franklin Roosevelt's early New Deal.
